title: Aurobindo's Savitri
hookLine: an old story you already know, retold as a legend and a symbol
carry: savitri's steady love wins life back from death

cards: A princess named Savitri chooses Satyavan for her husband, though she's told he will die within the year.
On the day it comes, they're in the forest together, he lays his head in her lap, and Death himself arrives to carry him off. And Savitri gets up and follows Death.
Earlier this year you heard that story as the Mahabharata tells it. Aurobindo heard something more in it, and turned it into a long poem of his own.

teach.b: He called the poem Savitri, and gave it a subtitle: a legend and a symbol. In a note at its front, he explains. The Mahabharata tells the tale as married love conquering death, and he doesn't deny that.
But he reads each person in it as standing for something larger too.

teach.h: SATYAVAN: THE SOUL, HELD BY DEATH.
teach.b: Satyavan is the soul that carries the divine truth inside it, but has come down into the grip of death and ignorance.

teach.h: SAVITRI: THE DIVINE WORD, COME TO SAVE.
teach.b: Savitri is the divine Word, daughter of the Sun, come down to be born and to save.
Her father, the king who prayed so long for a child, stands for tapasya, the long human effort that reaches from the mortal toward the immortal. Put that beside yesterday's four words.
If all life is yoga, and the divine comes down to change life rather than flee it, then Savitri is that hope told as a story. She doesn't climb out of the world to escape death.

She walks after Death, speaks to him of dharma, and won't let go until life is given back. His reading doesn't replace the old tale; it holds a second lamp up to it. And the old tale isn't only read, it's kept.

teach.h: VAT SAVITRI: A FAST, A BANYAN, A THREAD.
teach.b: Every year, in the month of Jyeshtha, many married Hindu women keep Vat Savitri: they fast, wind thread around a banyan tree, the tree where, as the tradition tells it, Satyavan lay with his head in her lap, and pray for their husbands' long life.
A wife's steadiness, kept as a vow.

how: On Vat Savitri, in the month of Jyeshtha, many married Hindu women fast, wind thread around a banyan tree and pray for their husbands' long life; some followers of Sri Aurobindo also read his Savitri aloud, a few lines at a time, as a daily spiritual reading.

Savitri's story is still kept today, at a banyan tree
on Vat Savitri, many married Hindu women fast and wind thread around a banyan in her memory, praying for their husbands' long life.
his Savitri escapes death by leaving the world behind
she walks after Death and won't let go until life is given back.

games.q: you're Savitri. Death has come into the forest and is carrying your husband away. what do you do?
o: accept it, and go home to mourn.
run to the village for help.
games.why: in the Mahabharata and in Aurobindo's poem alike, Savitri follows Death. for Aurobindo, that walk is the divine refusing to leave life in death's grip.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love whose life or health you worry about, and see them clearly, the way Savitri saw Satyavan with his head in her lap.
Then, with each breath, hold them steadily, without letting go, the way the women at the banyan wind the thread around it again and again.
If you pray, pray for their long life in your own words; if you don't, simply wish them well, breath by breath.

wordCard.voice: Aurobindo. The teacher who retold Savitri as a legend and a symbol: the soul held by death, and the divine come down to bring it back to life.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: Savitri, the princess of the Mahabharata tale and the title of Aurobindo's long poem.
